title: LP, QP, convex and nonlinear programs

sections.body_md:
Not every optimization problem is the same kind of object. A linear program has an affine objective and affine constraints. A quadratic program keeps the affine constraints and allows a quadratic objective. A convex program is the wider class in which the objective is a convex function and the feasible set is a convex set. Anything else is a general nonlinear program.

The quadratic case needs one algebraic cleanup. A square matrix and its symmetric part define the same quadratic form, because the skew part contributes nothing to \(x^T Q x\). Eigenvalue tests are run on the symmetric part. If that matrix is positive semidefinite, the quadratic objective is convex. If it is indefinite, the quadratic program is not a convex program, even when every constraint is linear.

Convexity is what makes a local solution enough. On a convex problem every local minimizer is global, so an algorithm that stops at a local solution has solved the problem. A nonconvex quadratic can bend up in one direction and down in another, and a point that is best nearby need not be best on the whole feasible set.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: The symmetric part of \(Q\) is \((Q + Q^T)/2\), and \(x^T Q x = x^T ((Q + Q^T)/2) x\). The form \(a x^2 + b xy + c y^2\) belongs to the symmetric matrix with diagonal entries \(a\) and \(c\) and off-diagonal entries \(b/2\). Its determinant is \(ac - b^2/4\). A quadratic objective with a positive semidefinite Hessian, and a convex feasible set, is a convex program. Affine inequalities define a convex set, so a quadratic program is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the form \(4x^2 + 14 xy + 9y^2\). The cross term is \(14xy\), so the symmetric matrix has off-diagonal entries \(7\) and diagonal entries \(4\) and \(9\). The symmetrized corner is 7. The determinant of that matrix is \(4\cdot 9 - 49 = -13\), which is negative, so the form is indefinite.

The same expression with the cross term removed, \(4x^2 + 9y^2\), has a diagonal Hessian of second derivatives with positive entries, and it is strictly convex. The cross term is the whole difference between a convex quadratic and an indefinite one. Symmetrizing did not create that difference. It only put the form into a matrix whose eigenvalues are allowed to decide.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A linear objective with a quadratic constraint is not a quadratic program. The quadratic piece has to sit in the objective, and the constraints have to stay affine. Reading eigenvalues of an unsymmetrized matrix answers a different question, because those eigenvalues need not even be real. A positive diagonal is not positive semidefiniteness: the matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(2\) and off-diagonal entries \(3\) has a negative determinant. Calling a problem convex because the objective is a square misses the feasible set. The complement of a disk is not convex.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Linear programs are rewritten in a standard form and then searched at basic feasible solutions. Convex quadratic programs include least-squares fits and the training problem of a linear classifier with a squared-norm objective. The second-order test for a local minimizer uses the same Hessian, and for a convex objective that local test becomes a global one.
